clue.text: High-flier scene?

parts.note: read as the social world of rich people who fly from one fashionable resort to the next

explanation.surface: A question about where high achievers gather.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the glamorous lifestyle of wealthy international travellers, who are literally high fliers.

clue.text: Dealer with valuable material for film partnership

parts.note: a dealer is a merchant, one who trades goods
ivory is a prized material from elephant tusks

explanation.surface: A trader in precious goods is linked with a cinema partnership.
explanation.walkthrough: Merchant Ivory was the film-making team of producer Ismail Merchant and director James Ivory.
explanation.definitionFit: The producer and director duo made period films together for decades under their joint names.

clue.text: Significant enough to tip the balance, say

definitions.text: enough to tip the balance, say

explanation.surface: Something big enough to make a difference on the scales.
explanation.definitionFit: A measurable change is a noticeable one; anything heavy enough to move a pair of scales can be weighed.

clue.text: Slowing down tenor and all in new composition

indicators.note: the words are put together afresh, rearranged into a different order

explanation.surface: A musical direction involving the tenor and the rest of the singers in a new piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in new composition' rearranges TENOR, AND and ALL; the musical surface hides that 'composition' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rallentando is the Italian musical direction meaning gradually getting slower.

clue.text: His ode needs translation

indicators.note: translating turns words into new forms, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet's ode must be translated for modern readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs translation' rearranges HIS and ODE; read whole, the clue describes the Greek poet, whose odes need translating.
explanation.definitionFit: Hesiod was an ancient Greek poet whose verse readers today meet in translation.

clue.text: Everything left on the table, we hear, in Warwickshire town

indicators.note: the phrase is said out loud and the sound gives the place name

parts.note: if everything is left on the table, none was eaten

explanation.surface: A meal untouched, mentioned in connection with a Midlands town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' says NONE EATEN aloud. Warwickshire is an English county in the Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuneaton is a market town in the north of the English county of Warwickshire.

clue.text: A case we brought from France

definitions.text: A case we brought from France

parts.words: A case we brought from France
parts.note: read as a travel bag whose name English took over from the French language

explanation.surface: Someone describes luggage carried home from a French trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a souvenir, but the clue means the word itself was borrowed from French, where it means a suitcase.
explanation.definitionFit: A valise is a small travelling bag, a word English borrowed from French.

clue.text: Humour is questionable, containing such a piece?

definitions.text: Humour is questionable, containing such a piece?

indicators.note: the words of the clue hold the run of letters within them, across the word breaks

explanation.surface: Doubtful humour may include a slightly rude item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'containing' points to the letters inside 'humouR IS QUEstionable'; read whole, the clue describes the near-the-knuckle humour the word means.
explanation.definitionFit: Risqué describes humour that is slightly indecent and so of questionable taste.

clue.text: Survey where pupil is in anatomy

explanation.surface: An inspection of a school pupil studying biology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pupil' looks like a schoolchild; in anatomy it is the dark opening at the centre of the iris.
explanation.definitionFit: To survey something is to look it over; the pupil of a person sits in the organ of sight.

clue.text: Fails to secure financial backer in US city

indicators.note: one word holds another safely inside it, as if locking it in

parts.note: to fail is to lose
an angel is an investor who backs a theatre show or venture

explanation.surface: A business that collapses without getting an investor in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to secure' puts ANGEL inside LOSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Los Angeles is the large Californian city, home of Hollywood.

clue.text: Girl returning, carrying one Mexican plant

indicators.note: the reversed word bears the other piece inside it
coming back means the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a lass is a girl
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A young woman comes home with a single cactus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns LASS into SSAL, and 'carrying' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is an agave from Mexico whose leaves yield fibre for rope.

clue.text: Apes needing fruit, lacking energy

indicators.note: being without something means a letter is removed

parts.note: oranges are a citrus fruit
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Monkeys in need of something to eat but feeling lethargic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' takes E out of ORANGES.
explanation.definitionFit: Orangs is the short form of orangutans, the red-haired great apes of Borneo and Sumatra.

clue.text: Go wrong in it, somehow achieving a good fit over time

definitions.text: achieving a good fit over time

indicators.note: some way or other means the letters are worked into a different order

explanation.surface: Making a mess of something yet coming to suit it eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges the letters of GO WRONG IN IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A child gradually fills out clothes bought too big, so they come to fit as the child develops.

clue.text: Having a sit-down when working to rule?

definitions.text: Having a sit-down when working to rule?

parts.words: Having a sit-down when working to rule?
parts.note: read as a monarch seated in state, whose work is literally ruling a kingdom

explanation.surface: Industrial action, where staff sit down or work to rule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sit-down' and 'working to rule' look like strike tactics, but they describe a monarch seated on the royal chair to reign.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone placed on the seat of state is enthroned, as a monarch is while ruling.

clue.text: Rise reduced by head of company, in old-fashioned fiddle

indicators.note: cut short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to rise up is to rebel

indicators.note: the head is the start of the word, its initial letter

explanation.surface: A company boss stops a pay increase for an antique violin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' trims REBEL to REBE, and 'head of' gives C from company.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebec is a medieval bowed string instrument, an ancestor of the violin.

clue.text: Game and fit, and not out of reach of the other side

definitions.text: not out of reach of the other side

parts.note: bridge is a card game
able means fit or capable

explanation.surface: A player who is game and fit can reach an opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like an adjective meaning willing, but it is the card game.
explanation.definitionFit: A river that can be spanned allows passage across to the far bank.

clue.text: Comrades as inebriated as these? They're soft drinks

indicators.note: drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: Friends who are as drunk as fizzy pop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inebriated' rearranges COMRADES AS; the joke is that these drinks would never make anyone drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream sodas are sweet vanilla-flavoured carbonated beverages without alcohol.

clue.text: Printed like crossword squares

explanation.surface: Something published, like the grid of a puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something set down in print is in black and white; a puzzle grid has dark and light cells.

clue.text: Repressed, didn't rise

explanation.surface: Someone held back who stayed low.
explanation.definitionFit: To repress is to hold under; anything that never got up stayed low.

clue.text: An all-consuming vice?

parts.note: read literally as the sin of wanting to eat or take everything

explanation.surface: A question about a passion that takes over one's life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all-consuming' usually means obsessive; here it literally means consuming everything, one of the seven deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice or gluttony is the desire to devour and possess more than is needed.

clue.text: Everyday objects for teaching religion classes, and others in Latin

parts.note: RE is religious education, a school subject in Britain
alia is Latin for other things

explanation.surface: Ordinary teaching aids used in RE and Latin lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the British school subject Religious Education.
explanation.definitionFit: Realia are real items such as coins or tools used in class to illustrate lessons.

clue.text: Like a great story, one set in strange place

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside another
odd, so the letters of the word are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A grand tale with one character in an odd location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges PLACE to EPCAL, and 'set in' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Epical means of the nature of an epic, the long heroic narrative.

clue.text: Successfully court, say, upper-class maiden — that's sweet

parts.note: to court someone successfully is to win them
e.g. means for example, as 'say' does
U is the label for upper-class usage
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A suitor wins over a posh young woman, and that is lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maiden' looks like a young woman; it is M, a cricket maiden (an over with no runs). A wine gum is a chewy British sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine gum is a fruity chewy confection, a type of candy.

clue.text: Complain about a partner in New Zealand

indicators.note: going around means one piece is wrapped round the other

parts.note: to whine is to complain

explanation.surface: Grumbling about a spouse while living in New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts WHINE around A.
explanation.definitionFit: Wahine is a Maori word for a woman or wife, used in New Zealand English.

clue.text: Trap I demolished, filled with love, as Shakespearean heroine

indicators.note: the rearranged letters take in another piece inside them
knocked down, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A snare broken apart and full of affection, fit for a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'demolished' rearranges TRAP I to PRTIA, and 'filled with' puts O inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Portia is the heroine of The Merchant of Venice who argues the case in disguise.

clue.text: State in which I had turned old

indicators.note: turned round, so the word is read backwards

explanation.surface: A place where someone grew old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses HAD to DAH.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is one of the fifty US states, in the north-west.

clue.text: Crazy proposal that'll change your position

parts.note: loco is slang for crazy
a motion is a proposal put to a meeting

explanation.surface: A mad suggestion that would shift your stance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'position' looks like an opinion; it means physical place.
explanation.definitionFit: Locomotion is movement from one place to another.

clue.text: Piece of arable acreage

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is taken, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: A plot of farmland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of' takes the letters from 'arabLE Acreage'; the whole clue also describes a stretch of grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: A lea is a meadow or tract of open land.

clue.text: Run after unusually lean beast, one found in Africa

indicators.note: the running piece comes behind the rearranged letters
in an unusual way, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: to lope is to run with long strides

explanation.surface: A thin animal is chased across the savanna.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' rearranges LEAN and BEAST, and 'after' puts LOPE at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The sable antelope is a large dark horned grazer of the southern African savanna.
